title: Distant opposition
summary: King and pawn against king: the opposition from afar, along the diagonal and along the rank, in defence, with spare tempi, and how it leads to the key square.
part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: With the kings far apart, the opposition is taken from afar and, with every step of the other king, turns into direct opposition.
step.t_lesson: The key squares of the g3 pawn are far from both kings. Think: if the white king runs straight for them, does the black king get there first? What is the right first step?
step.t_lesson.hint1: Put the kings on the same file and count the squares between them.
step.t_lesson.hint2: With an odd number of squares between the kings and the other side to move, the opposition is yours.
step.intro: The key squares of the g3-pawn are f5, g5 and h5, and if I just run there, the black king arrives first and stands in front. What decides it is opposition from afar: kings on the same file, an odd number of squares between them, one, three or five, and the other side to move. Capablanca puts it the other way round: with an even number of squares between them, the player to move takes the opposition.
step.d_distant: Watch distant opposition turn into direct opposition, one step at a time.
step.d_distant.m1: 1.Ke4. The black king's file, three squares in between, e5, e6 and e7, and The distant opposition is mine.
step.d_distant.m2: The black king cannot pass. He leaves the e-file for the f-file.
step.d_distant.m3: 2.Kf5. I go to the new file and stand in front of him, one square in between. And f5 is already a key square of the g3-pawn.
step.d_distant.m4: He gives way again, now to the g-file.
step.d_distant.m5: 3.Kg5. Face to face again, on another key square. From here the pawn queens.
step.convert: This time the black king will answer differently. Take the distant opposition and, after each of his moves, face him until you reach the key square.
step.convert.hint: 1.Ke4 first. If the black king stays on the e-file, face him; when he leaves it, go to the new file, face to face.
step.convert.done: That's it: from afar, face to face, and the key square. With the king on f5 the pawn queens.
part.diagonal.title: Along the diagonal
part.diagonal.summary: When the file is out of reach, the opposition also works along a diagonal.
step.t_diagonal: The black king guards the key squares of the e3-pawn, and the white king's most natural move looks good, but it may not be. Which square leaves the black king without a good answer?
step.t_diagonal.hint1: The kings need not be on the same file: a diagonal works too, with one square between them.
step.t_diagonal.hint2: After coming in along the diagonal, wherever the black king goes, look to face him again, from any side.
step.diagonal: So far the kings were on the same file. Now they are not, and the bridge is the diagonal. 1.Ke4 looks natural, but after 1...Ke6 it is the black king that has direct opposition, and the e3-pawn does not get through. The way in is 1.Kf4: the diagonal f4, e5, d6, one square in between, and From then on I always stand facing him, from above or from the side.
step.d_diagonal: Watch the diagonal turn into direct opposition.
step.d_diagonal.m1: 1.Kf4. Kings on the diagonal f4, e5, d6, one square in between, and
step.d_diagonal.m2: The black king goes to e6, in front of the pawn, to block the e-file.
step.d_diagonal.m3: 2.Ke4. Now face to face on the e-file, one square in between: direct opposition, and
step.d_diagonal.m4: He has to give way. He goes to d6, from where he still guards d5 and e5.
step.d_diagonal.m5: 3.Kf5. The key square that was left free. With the king here, the e3-pawn queens.
step.diagonalMove: Come in along the diagonal; this time the black king will answer differently.
step.diagonalMove.hint: 1.Kf4. If the black king comes to d5, face him along the rank.
step.diagonalMove.done: 2.Kf5: kings on d5 and f5, one square in between, and That is opposition along the rank, and f5 is a key square. It comes back shortly.
part.defend.title: In defence
part.defend.summary: The defender uses the same rule: take the opposition from afar, even by stepping back, and follow the attacking king.
step.t_carlsenSo: White has two pawns against one, and the white king wants to get in. Only one move draws. Which?
step.t_carlsenSo.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the f-file.
step.t_carlsenSo.hint2: Two squares in between is an even number: on the move, you can make it odd, even by stepping back.
step.defend: So far the side with the opposition was attacking. Now it defends, in a real game: Carlsen against Wesley So, Norway Chess, Stavanger, 2017. The knights came off on move 53, and So was a pawn down. The white king is on f3, the black king on f6, two squares in between, and So is to move. 55...Ke6 or 55...Kg6 would let the white king take the opposition and get in. So stepped back: 55...Kf7, three squares in between and The opposition is his, and it serves the defence.
step.d_carlsenSo: The moves of the game. For the white king's first three steps, So stays on the same file, three squares above.
step.d_carlsenSo.m1: 55...Kf7! He steps back and takes the distant opposition: f4, f5 and f6 in between, and
step.d_carlsenSo.m2: Carlsen changes file, trying to get round the side.
step.d_carlsenSo.m3: 56...Ke7! So changes file with him: three squares in between again, now on the e-file.
step.d_carlsenSo.m4: Carlsen tries the d-file. If So does not follow now, he loses: 57...Kd7 is again the only move.
step.d_carlsenSo.m5: 57...Kd7! Facing him again, from afar. The white king moves, but gains no ground.
step.d_carlsenSo.m6: Carlsen goes up the c-file, to come in from the queenside.
step.d_carlsenSo.m7: 58...Ke6! The black king comes back close to the pawns, and the white king has no way in. The game was drawn on move 63.
step.defendMove: Now with a single pawn: take the distant opposition and, when the white king comes up, face him.
step.defendMove.hint: 1...Kf7. If the white king goes to e4, go to e6; if he pushes the pawn, come back to f6.
step.defendMove.done: 1...Kf7 from afar, 2...Ke6 face to face, and after 3.g4 the king comes back to f6 and occupies the key square the white king wanted. The same thing So did against two pawns.
part.lateral.title: Sideways, along the rank
part.lateral.summary: The opposition also works along a rank, near and far, in attack and in defence.
step.t_euwe: Your king wants the a5-pawn; the black king wants to run to your c2-pawn. Only one move wins. Which?
step.t_euwe.hint1: The kings can face each other sideways, on the same rank.
step.t_euwe.hint2: Count the squares between the kings on the fifth rank after your move.
step.lateral: So far the kings faced each other head on or along the diagonal; now, sideways. Euwe against Whitaker, The Hague Olympiad, 1928. The rooks came off on move 47, and this was left. Euwe played 49.Kb5: it attacks the a5-pawn and puts the kings on the fifth rank, three squares in between and That is distant opposition along the rank: when the black king goes down towards the c2-pawn, the white king goes down with him, sideways, and gets there first.
step.d_euwe: The moves of the game: Euwe always stays on the black king's rank.
step.d_euwe.m1: 49.Kb5! The only winning move. Kings on b5 and f5, three squares in between, and
step.d_euwe.m2: Whitaker heads down towards the c2-pawn.
step.d_euwe.m3: 50.Kxa5! The pawn falls, and the kings again have three squares in between, a5 and e5, with
step.d_euwe.m4: He goes further down and threatens 51...Kc3, attacking the c2-pawn.
step.d_euwe.m5: 51.Kb4! Kings on b4 and d4, one square in between, and Black to move: lateral opposition, and c3 is shut to him.
step.d_euwe.m6: With no way through c3, he steps back. Every move loses: the white king is already in front of the pawn.
step.d_euwe.m7: 52.Kb5. The white king goes up in front of the pawn, towards b6 and c6. Euwe went on with 53.c4, 54.Kb6 and 55.Kc6, and the game ended there, a win for White.
step.lateralDefend: The white king will come down to support the d2-pawn; come down with him, sideways, and get there first.
step.lateralDefend.hint: 1...Ke6: a6 and e6, three squares in between. Then, after each of his steps, stay on the same rank with one square in between.
step.lateralDefend.done: 1...Ke6, 2...Kd5, 3...Kd4: you came down sideways and reached the key squares of the pawn, c4, d4 and e4, first. Sometimes the move that takes the opposition goes sideways, sometimes backwards, like So's 55...Kf7.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: Locked pawns on both sides: distant opposition leads to outflanking, and outflanking to the other side's pawn.
step.t_capablanca: Locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever reaches an enemy pawn first wins. Think: which white king move makes sure of getting there first?
step.t_capablanca.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the e-file. With an even number, the side to move can take the opposition.
step.t_capablanca.hint2: Six squares in between and your move: after your move an odd number must be left.
step.capablanca: Now there are pawns on both sides, and the target is not queening: it is the other side's pawn. This is the example Capablanca chose, in Chess Fundamentals, to show the value of the opposition. Each side has two blocked pawns, b4 against b5 and h4 against h5, and the kings are on e1 and e8, with six squares between them. An even number: whoever is to move takes the opposition, and whoever takes the opposition wins, because he reaches the other side's pawn first. 1.Ke2 is the only move that wins.
step.d_capablanca: Watch what the opposition gives you here: the outflanking.
step.d_capablanca.m2: The black king comes down the file.
step.d_capablanca.m3: 2.Ke3. Three squares in between, and he is still the one to move.
step.d_capablanca.m4: He comes forward again: two squares in between, and it is my move.
step.d_capablanca.m5: 3.Ke4. Direct opposition, one square in between: now Black has to leave the file.
step.d_capablanca.m6: He gives way towards the h5-pawn.
step.d_capablanca.m7: 4.Kf4! Face to face again, on the f-file, and the h4-pawn stays protected. 4.Kd5? would race for b5 and only draw: the black king would capture the h4-pawn in time.
step.d_capablanca.m8: He gives way again, to g6, to guard the h5-pawn. The e-file is now free.
step.d_capablanca.m9: 5.Ke5! The outflanking: the black king went to one side, and the white king goes past on the other. From here it heads for d5 and c5, the b5-pawn falls, and the black king is too far from b4.
step.capablancaMove: Take the distant opposition and, when the black king leaves the file, do not follow him: step forward on the other side and take the opposition again.
step.capablancaMove.hint: 1.Ke2 first. After 1...Kf8, 2.Ke3 would be a mistake: 2...Ke7 would follow, with the opposition for Black. Step sideways and forward, 2.Kd3, and wait for the black king to come back to the e-file. On the first move, 1.Kd1 and 1.Kf1 lose, and 1.Kd2 and 1.Kf2 only draw.
step.capablancaMove.done: Exactly. 1.Ke2, and after 1...Kf8 the sidestep 2.Kd3, the mirror image of the 2.Kf3 Capablanca gives against 1...Kd8 (2.Kf2 works too, keeping five squares in between). When the black king came back to e7, 3.Ke3 took the opposition again with three squares in between. From here the white king goes to the b5-pawn or the h5-pawn, whichever Black leaves.
part.edge.title: Up to the edge
part.edge.summary: The kings climb side by side; at the top, the attacking king uses the edge to gain the move and get round.
step.t_edge: The goal is to win, and the target is the c6-pawn. 1.Kd6 looks like the shortest way. Is it?
step.t_edge.hint1: After 1.Kd6, where does the black king stand, and whose move is it?
step.t_edge.hint2: The kings are on the fifth rank; count the squares between them.
step.edge: In the previous chapter the outflanking happened in the middle of the board; now it happens at the edge. This is a training position on distant opposition. 1.Kd6? Kb6! and the kings stand side by side, one square in between, with White to move: the white king does not get through, and it is a draw. The right move is to step away: 1.Kf5. That leaves four squares in between, from a5 to f5, and Black to move, but the black king cannot stay on the fifth rank: b5 is covered by the c4-pawn. He has to go up, and I go up with him, three squares in between. Then the kings climb together, side by side, and at the top I use the edge to gain the move.
step.d_edge: Watch the kings climb side by side.
step.d_edge.m1: 1.Kf5! I step away: a5 and f5, four squares in between, and The black king cannot answer on b5, which the c4-pawn covers.
step.d_edge.m2: The black king has to leave the fifth rank: b5 and b4 are covered by the c4- and a3-pawns. He goes up.
step.d_edge.m3: 2.Kf6. I go up with him: b6 and f6, three squares in between, and he is to move. The c6-pawn stands on one of them, but it counts just the same.
step.d_edge.m4: He goes up to b7, and I go up with him to keep three squares in between on the same rank.
step.d_edge.m5: 3.Kf7. Seventh rank, three squares in between, and he is still the one to move.
step.d_edge.m6: He goes back to b6. If I go to e7 now, he goes up to b7 and the opposition becomes his.
step.d_edge.m7: 4.Ke8! The waiting square: from here, wherever he goes on the seventh rank, I take the opposition along the rank on the next move.
step.d_edge.m8: He goes to a7. On b7, 5.Kd7 would leave him side by side with one square in between; on c7, 5.Ke7 would do the same.
step.d_edge.m9: 5.Ke7! a7 and e7, three squares in between, and He will have to give way, and my king gets into d7 or d6 and on to the c6-pawn.
step.edgeMove: This time the black king answers differently.
step.edgeMove.hint: 1.Kf5 first. If Black stays on the sixth rank, come closer along the sixth and stand beside him with him to move.
step.edgeMove.done: Kings on the sixth rank with Black to move: the lateral opposition is yours, and the black king will have to leave c6.
part.reserve.title: The spare tempo
part.reserve.summary: A free pawn move passes the turn and hands the opposition to the other side.
step.t_reserve: This is Capablanca's example with an extra white pawn on a2, and Without the a2-pawn, the side to move wins. And now?
step.t_reserve.hint1: Who has a move that changes nothing between the kings?
step.t_reserve.hint2: A pawn move passes the turn, and the turn decides the opposition.
step.reserve: So far the kings were the ones deciding. Now the free pawn comes in. Without the a2-pawn, Black would play 1...Ke7 and win: distant opposition. With the a2-pawn, 1...Ke7 is met by 2.a3. The pawn moved, the kings did not, and the move is back with Black. A free pawn move is a spare tempo: whoever has one decides who has the opposition. That is why, when it is the other side that has the spare tempo, taking the opposition early is no use: he passes the turn with the pawn.
step.d_reserve: Watch the spare tempo hand the opposition over.
step.d_reserve.m1: Black takes the distant opposition, five squares in between. Without the a2-pawn, Black would win.
step.d_reserve.m2: 2.a3. The pawn passes the turn: the kings have not moved, and now it is Black who must move with five squares in between. The opposition has changed hands.
step.d_reserve.m3: The black king comes forward. Four squares in between, and it is my move: an even number, the player to move takes the opposition.
step.d_reserve.m4: 3.Ke2. Three squares in between, and Here it is the only winning move.
step.d_reserve.m5: He comes forward again: two squares in between, and I am to move.
step.d_reserve.m6: 4.Ke3. Direct opposition, and Black to move: the black king will have to give way, and mine gets round him as in Capablanca's example.
step.grigorievMove: A study by Grigoriev, 1930. Your two pawns hold waiting moves: spend each one at the right moment.
step.grigorievMove.hint: Start with 1.b3. After 1...Ka5, do not come closer yet: 2.Ka7 and 2.Kb7 let 2...b4 draw. Stay a step away and wait for Black's pawn move; after 2...b4, 3.c4 is your waiting move.
step.grigorievMove.done: 1.b3, 2.Kb8 and 3.c4. 2.Kb8 stayed a step away: Black had 2...b4 in reserve and had to spend it first. Then your 3.c4 passed the turn, and the kings walk side by side, along the eighth and sixth ranks, until the black king gives way. That is how Grigoriev solved the study.
part.means.title: A means, not an end
part.means.summary: The opposition is there to reach the key square or the pawn. If you can get there without it, do.
step.t_means: 1.Ke4 takes direct opposition. Is it the move?
step.t_means.hint1: Where are the key squares of the c4-pawn? Can you reach them without going through the opposition?
step.means: So far the opposition decided everything. A warning to close with: it is a means, not an end. In this position, 1.Ke4 takes direct opposition and only draws: the black king answers 1...Kd6, and you do not get through. 1.Kc5 ignores the opposition and goes straight to the door of the key squares b6, c6 and d6. If you can get in without it, get in. In Grigoriev's studies in the test, the target is sometimes a pawn on the other side: count who gets there first.
step.d_means: Watch the white king go straight to the key square.
step.d_means.m1: 1.Kc5! No opposition at all: the king goes to the door, with b6 and d6 within reach.
step.d_means.m2: The black king tries to block from the d-side.
step.d_means.m3: 2.Kb6. A key square of the c4-pawn. From here the pawn queens.
step.d_means.m4: He goes in front of the pawn.
step.d_means.m5: 3.Kc6. I take away b7, c7 and d7: the black king only has the eighth rank.
step.d_means.m6: He only has b8 and d8. He goes to b8, and c8 is within my king's reach.
step.d_means.m7: 4.Kd7. I control c8, and the pawn walks to queen on its own.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: kings on the same file, rank or diagonal, with one, three or five squares between them and the other side to move, you have the opposition; it works in attack and in defence, head on, sideways or stepping back. Second: before taking the opposition, count the waiting pawn moves on both sides, which pass the turn. Third: the opposition is a means; the end is the key square or the pawn, and when the other king gives way, go past on the other side.
step.finish: Now play until you queen. Your pawn is far from the kings: find the distant opposition, follow the black king and take yours to the key squares of the f2-pawn.
ex.e09: The black king stands in front of the key squares and yours is in the corner. Find the winning move.
ex.e09.hint: First the black king's file, from afar. Then, every time he moves, shorten the distance facing him.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Kg2! takes the distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares in between. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf3! After 2...Ke6, 3.Ke4! And after 3...Kd6, 4.Kd4! Every step keeps the number odd, down to direct opposition beside the pawn. Starting with the pawn or with another king move draws.
ex.e11: The white pawn is still on the second rank, and the white king is far away. Only one move holds.
ex.e11.hint: The white king is on e1. Get onto his file and, with every step he takes, face him, even if he changes file.
ex.e11.solution: 1...Ke7! Kings on e1 and e7, five squares between them, White to move: the distant opposition is yours. After 2.Kd2, 2...Kd6!, with three squares between; after 3.Kd3, 3...Kd5!, face to face; and after 4.Kc3, 4...Kc5! The white king never reaches the key squares of the c2-pawn, b4, c4 and d4. Any other first move lets the white king take the opposition, and at every step of the defence only one move holds.
ex.e13: Black has two pawns against one, and the black king wants to come in along the second rank to win the e3-pawn. Only one move holds.
ex.e13.hint: The kings are on the same rank. The opposition also works sideways and from afar: count the squares between them.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kg1! Kings on c1 and g1, three squares between them, d1, e1 and f1, and Black to move: the distant opposition along the rank is yours. After 1...Kd2, 2.Kf2!, side by side with one square between; after 2...Kd3, 3.Kf3! The black king never sets foot on e2 or e4, and the e3-pawn stays. 1.Kf2? looks more active, but after 1...Kd2 it is your move and Black has the opposition; 2.Kf1? loses to 2...Kd1! Capablanca shows the same defence, with the pawns one file further right, in example 28 of Chess Fundamentals.
ex.e14: A study by Nikolai Grigoriev, 1933. White to play and win. Black keeps a pawn move in reserve to pass the move.
ex.e14.hint: With the black king on b4, you want yours on b2 with Black to move. Going to b2 at once gives Black the chance to answer with the pawn. Stay one step away from b2.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Ka1!! 1.Kb2? is already direct opposition against the king on b4, but 1...d4! passes the move, and you are the one who has to give way. From a1, if 1...d4, 2.Kb2! and the opposition belongs to White. After 1...Kc3, 2.Kb1! After 2...Kb4, 3.Kc1 (a1 and a2 also do); after 3...Kc3, 4.Kd1! (or 4.Kb1). When the pawn finally advances, 4...d4 5.Kc1 d3 6.cxd3 Kxd3, your king goes to b2, in front of the b3-pawn, and wins. On the first move, 1.Kb1, 1.Kb2, 1.c3+ and 1.c4 only draw.
ex.e15: A study by Nikolai Grigoriev, 1932. White to play and win. The black king wants to get back to the queenside and win your pawns.
ex.e15.hint: The kings will climb side by side, each on its own file. Your pawns hold waiting moves: spend each one only when it passes the move at the right moment.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kg4!, and after 1...Ke3, 2.c3! The pawn leaves the black king's reach and keeps its second step, c4, for later. The kings climb side by side, 3.Kg5 Ke5, 4.Kg6 Ke6, 5.Kg7 Ke7, with one square between them and White to move: the opposition along the rank is Black's. But on the seventh rank the black king has nowhere higher to go, and 6.c4! passes the move (stepping back with 6.Kg6 also wins, but only postpones the decision). After 6...Ke6, 7.Kf8! and 8.Ke7 go round the black king and reach the c5-pawn first. On the first move, 1.c3 allows 1...Kf3 with the opposition for Black; on the second, 2.c4 lets the black king come back.
ex.e16: A study by Nikolai Grigoriev, 1929. White to play and draw. The kings are on the same file, with six squares between them.
ex.e16.hint: 1.Ke2 would take the distant opposition, but the fight is not on the e-file: the black king will go round by the queenside to the e5-pawn. Think about your king's target and which square it must be on when the black king reaches e5.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kf2!! 1.Ke2? takes the opposition and loses: 1...Kd7!, 2...Kc6, 3...Kb5, and the black king goes round. 1.h6? loses to 1...Kf7. The white king's target is the h7-pawn: after 1...Kd7, 2.h6! fixes it, and the king heads for the kingside, always in step with the black king: 2...Kc6 3.Kg3!, 3...Kd5 4.Kh4!, 4...Kd4 5.Kh5!, 5...Ke4 6.Kg4!, 6...Kxe5 7.Kg5! In the last two moves the kings stand on the same rank, side by side, with one square between them and Black to move: the black king gives way, and the white one reaches f6 and the h7-pawn. If 1...Ke7, 2.Kf3!!, for the same reason. Every white move in the line is the only one that draws.
key.lesson: The white king takes the opposition from far away, with several squares between the kings, and closes the gap step by step until it reaches the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.diagonal: The opposition works along the diagonal too: the white king stands on the same diagonal as the black king and, step by step, turns it into face-to-face opposition.
key.means: The opposition is a means, not the goal: here taking it only draws. What wins is taking the king straight to the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.capablanca: Capablanca's example: locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever is to move takes the distant opposition and wins.
key.carlsenSo: Carlsen–So, Norway Chess, Stavanger, 2017: Black to move. 55...Kf7! steps back and takes the distant opposition; So followed the white king from file to file and drew. Moves from PGN Mentor.
key.euweWhitaker: Euwe–Whitaker, The Hague Olympiad, 1928: White to move. 49.Kb5! takes the distant opposition along the fifth rank, 51.Kb4! the direct lateral one, and White won. Moves from PGN Mentor.
history: The opposition is the kings' struggle over who has to give way, and it doesn't only happen with the kings close together: it can start from far away, with several squares between them, or even along a diagonal. Whoever understands this wins pawn endings that look drawn and saves others that look lost. It looks simple and isn't: taking the opposition at the wrong moment, or treating it as the goal, throws the game away. The man who explained the opposition to ordinary players was the Cuban José Raúl Capablanca, world champion, in his 1921 book Chess Fundamentals, with an example of locked pawns that still appears in manuals today. Decades later the Russian Yuri Averbakh added the reminder this lesson repeats: the opposition is a means; the goal is to put the king on the squares that decide.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3, and the black king on e6, in front of the key squares. Find the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
